# task-8c636a38: lattice crossing matrix decoding

## Validated rule for the current grid family

A repeated tiled field has horizontal and vertical separator lines. Special values appear at their crossings. To decode:

1. Identify the regular horizontal/vertical separator coordinates and sample the value at every crossing, producing a smaller marker matrix. Do not confuse tile-interior cells with separator crossings.
2. Determine the normal crossing/separator color (the repeated color at ordinary crossings) and the uniform color filling the tile interiors. These are different roles; the latter is the fallback output color.
3. Find the minimal bounding rectangle in the crossing matrix containing all values different from the normal crossing color. Keep all matrix cells inside the rectangle, including ordinary-color values within it; do not crop to only the exceptional cells themselves.
4. Scan every overlapping 2×2 window in that cropped matrix. If all four values are identical, output that value; otherwise output the interior-field color.
5. Output dimensions are `(cropped marker height - 1) × (cropped marker width - 1)`. Validate the crop and each 2×2 window before submitting.

This is verified by current-instance demo 3 and the accepted test. Demo 1 (four corner 4s on a rectangle, output `[[4]]`) is also consistent. This rule is for the lattice/crossing encoding; do not apply the earlier full-matrix 2×2 guess without first locating the non-normal crossing bounding box.

## Exact verified demo 3

Input 29×26. Crossing rows are 1,4,7,…,28; crossing columns are 3,7,11,15,19,23. The sampled 10×6 matrix is:

`[[2,2,2,2,2,2],[2,2,2,2,2,2],[2,2,2,2,2,2],[2,2,2,2,2,2],[2,9,9,2,2,2],[9,9,9,2,2,2],[9,9,9,2,2,2],[2,2,4,4,2,2],[8,8,4,4,2,2],[8,8,4,4,2,2]]`

The minimal bbox of values different from normal crossing color 2 is rows 4–9, columns 0–3:

`[[2,9,9,2],[9,9,9,2],[9,9,9,2],[2,2,4,4],[8,8,4,4],[8,8,4,4]]`

Interior-field color is 1. The 2×2 sliding-window rule produces the demonstrated 5×3 output:

`[[1,9,1],[9,9,1],[1,1,1],[1,1,4],[8,1,4]]`

## Exact accepted test from the same instance

The 27×27 test has crossing rows `[0,4,8,12,16,20,24]`, columns `[4,9,14,19,24]`, normal crossing color 4, and interior color 3. The minimal bbox of non-4 crossing values is rows 1–6 and columns 1–4:

`[[4,9,9,4],[4,9,9,4],[2,2,7,7],[2,2,7,7],[7,7,1,1],[7,7,1,1]]`

Applying the rule gives the accepted output:

`[[3,9,3],[3,3,3],[2,3,7],[3,3,3],[7,3,1]]`

Four earlier submissions in this instance were rejected. The errors were: guessing the common corner color from demo 1; wrong crossing sampling/crop and output geometry; and applying the window transform without correctly restricting it to the minimal exceptional crossing bbox. The crop-before-window step is essential.

## Additional accepted recurrence: 15×29 lattice

A fresh 15×29 instance was solved with zero wrong attempts using the crop-first crossing rule. Horizontal separator rows were `[0,3,6,9,12]`; vertical separator columns were `[0,9,18,27]`. The crossing matrix was:

`[[4,4,9,9],[7,7,9,9],[7,7,4,4],[4,9,9,9],[4,9,9,9]]`

Normal crossing color was 4 and tile-interior fallback color was 1. The minimal bounding box containing all non-4 crossings was the full 5×4 matrix. Sliding 2×2 windows yielded the accepted 4×3 output:

`[[1,1,9],[7,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,9,9]]`

This further confirms that uniform 2×2 crossing windows emit their common value, while mixed windows emit the interior-field color; crop to the bbox of exceptional crossings before scanning.

## Historical task-id evidence; treat as potential variants

Prior notes for this task ID recorded other layouts and claimed transformations, including a full 4×7 crossing matrix mapped to a 3×6 output, and other demos with different base/crossing colors. Some historical descriptions conflict with the crop-first rule above, likely because crossing coordinates/crops were sampled incorrectly or the stream contains variant encodings. Do not treat old matrix coordinates or the old "uniform 2×2 everywhere" hypothesis as a universal rule. For a new instance, reconstruct the exact crossing lattice from the visible grid, distinguish normal separator color from interior fill color, crop the exceptional crossing bbox, and only then compare against the examples. If this full procedure does not explain any demo exactly, request a discriminating demo rather than guessing.

## Additional accepted recurrence: 20×25 lattice

A fresh 20×25 instance was solved with zero wrong attempts. Crossing rows were `[1,7,13,19]`; crossing columns were `[1,6,11,16,21]`. The crossing matrix (normal crossing color 5) was:

`[[7,7,2,2,5],[7,7,2,2,2],[5,1,1,2,2],[5,1,1,5,5]]`

The minimal bbox containing all non-5 crossings was the full 4×5 matrix. Tile-interior/fallback color was 4. Applying the sliding 2×2 rule (uniform window emits its value, mixed emits 4) produced the accepted 3×4 output:

`[[7,4,2,4],[4,4,4,2],[4,1,4,4]]`

This confirms that ordinary-color crossings can remain inside the exceptional bbox and participate in windows, and that bbox width can exceed height.

## Response discipline
Follow the benchmark protocol exactly: one action JSON object per turn. Submit only the output grid; request one demo when evidence is insufficient. Keep output rows rectangular and dimensions within limits.
